title: A Permission Is Not A Path
subtitle: Module 08 — Service identity, the two data planes, and how a Pod actually gets its address

meta.note: Timing comes from the synthesised audio. estSeconds is a planning estimate only. Content authority: assets/content.js unit u8.

beats.title: You are here
beats.narration: DNS resolves, the ClusterIP times out, and nothing in the workload is wrong. This is the CNI segment of the request path. It covers how a Pod gets a network, and how a Service address becomes a real backend. It covers why a NetworkPolicy grants permission rather than a route. By the end you can split a connectivity failure into the layer that owns it.

visual.spec: REUSE spineLocator with segment eight lit.

beats.title: Three owners, not one network
beats.narration: Pod reachability and Service identity are two problems, and three owners share them. The network implementation configures Pod reachability, and CNI is the execution contract it is invoked through. The EndpointSlice controller records selector-matched backends and their conditions. kube-proxy, or a data plane replacing it, turns Service addresses into backend traffic. Three owners, three failure modes, three sets of logs.

visual.spec: NEW. Three labelled owners across the stage, each with what it owns and how it fails: CNI (Pod address and routes → no address, ContainerCreating), EndpointSlice (which backends are ready → empty slice, no backends), kube-proxy or eBPF (Service address to backend → rules not programmed, connection times out). Each owner's failure text is the point of the beat — give it the same weight as the owner name, not a footnote.

beats.title: Labels select, readiness conditions
beats.narration: For a selector Service, label matching is what puts a Pod address into an EndpointSlice. Readiness does something different. It sets that endpoint's ready condition. An unready address stays in the slice with ready false, and Service data planes normally avoid it. Setting publishNotReadyAddresses changes that behaviour. So a readiness probe does not add or remove an address. It changes a condition.

visual.spec: REUSE the pilot's Endpoints. Extend it: three Pods, one not ready. Show the ready gate admitting two addresses into the EndpointSlice and holding the third out. Then flip the third to ready and let its address appear in the slice, and only then let traffic reach it. Make the causal order visible — list first, traffic second. CORRECTION: membership comes from label matching, not readiness. Draw the unready address INSIDE the slice with ready:false, and the data plane declining to use it. Do not draw the address being held outside the slice.

beats.title: When the Service steps out
beats.narration: Setting clusterIP to None removes the Service virtual IP. DNS returns endpoint records instead, and kube-proxy does not handle that Service at all. The client or its resolver then chooses an endpoint, so balancing depends entirely on client behaviour. StatefulSet per-Pod DNS is built on exactly this.

visual.spec: NEW. Two queries side by side against the same backends. Left, a normal ClusterIP: one virtual address returned, traffic passes through the data plane, spread across backends. Right, clusterIP None: the full list of Pod addresses returned to the client, no data plane in the path, and the client connecting to the first entry every time. Label the right side with what it enables (stable per-Pod names) and what it costs (no balancing). CORRECTION: do not show 'client picks the first' as universal behaviour. Show the client choosing, with selection explicitly depending on the resolver and application.

beats.title: A permission is not a path
beats.narration: A matching ingress rule permits the flow at the destination. An isolating egress policy at the source has to permit it too, because policies combine additively. And a policy creates no route at all. podSelector chooses the Pods a policy protects. An empty podSelector with no ingress rules is default-deny ingress. If your network implementation does not enforce NetworkPolicy, the API stores the object with no enforcement status.

visual.spec: NEW. A NetworkPolicy object drawn as a permit stamp, not a pipe. Show it granting permission while the route underneath is missing — traffic still fails, and the policy is still green. Then the worse case: a plugin with no NetworkPolicy support. The API accepts the object, nothing enforces it, and the cluster looks protected while being open. Draw the accepted-but-ignored state explicitly; it is the beat. CORRECTION: core NetworkPolicy has no enforcement status, so do not draw a green enforced state. Show the destination-side permit and a separate source-side egress policy that must also allow the flow.

beats.title: Implementations, not APIs
beats.narration: iptables, IPVS and nftables are kube-proxy modes on Linux. An eBPF data plane is a separate implementation that can replace kube-proxy entirely. Your Service manifest usually stays the same across them, though behaviour depends on the implementation. The Service types stay constant too. ClusterIP exposes inside the cluster, NodePort adds a port on every node, LoadBalancer asks an external implementation for one. All three still use endpoints.

visual.spec: REUSE the pilot's DataPlane. Extend it: one unchanged Service manifest at the top feeding four interchangeable implementations below — iptables, IPVS, nftables, eBPF. Swap the implementation underneath while the manifest stays visibly identical. Do not rank them here; that is the next beat.

beats.title: Past the O(1) slogan
beats.narration: Someone will say IPVS is order one and iptables is order N. The slogan is right about lookup and incomplete as a recommendation. Kubernetes 1.35 deprecated kube-proxy's IPVS mode. It still runs in 1.36 and warns at startup, and nftables is the recommended Linux replacement. Compare data planes on lookup cost, update cost under churn, locality, kernel support and Service semantics.

visual.spec: NEW. Start with the slogan as a two-row comparison, then expand it into a multi-axis table the slogan omits: lookup cost, rule update cost under churn, locality, kernel version, semantics. Show the naive comparison shrinking into one column of a wider table. Every axis label must be legible — this beat is the correction, so the added axes carry it.

beats.title: The requirement does not go away
beats.narration: A related claim: that an eBPF data plane removes connection tracking. Separate the implementation from the requirement. Something still has to remember which connection a returning packet belongs to. Some implementations replace netfilter conntrack with BPF maps. Others keep kernel conntrack for certain traffic or modes. Check the product, and check the mode.

visual.spec: NEW. The requirement drawn once, in the centre and unchanged: 'remember which flow this packet belongs to'. Two implementations beneath it holding the same state — netfilter conntrack table, and BPF maps. Animate the state moving from one to the other while the requirement above stays fixed. The fixed requirement is the argument. CORRECTION: do not show a universal migration. Show it as implementation-dependent — some products move state to BPF maps, others keep kernel conntrack for some traffic or modes.

beats.title: A program, not a service
beats.narration: A CNI plugin is a program, not a service. The runtime sets CNI_COMMAND in the environment, writes JSON configuration to the plugin's standard input, and reads a JSON result from its standard output. Then the plugin exits. It runs in the host network domain, not inside the container. Products like Calico and Cilium also run a node agent, and that agent is not the plugin.

visual.spec: REUSE the pilot's CniExec, which already draws the exec contract. Extend it: show the plugin as a short-lived process that starts, is handed CNI_COMMAND plus stdin config, returns JSON on stdout, and exits. Beside it, a long-running node agent drawn as a separate process the short-lived binary talks to. The distinction between the two is the beat — do not merge them.

beats.title: The kubelet does not call it
beats.narration: The kubelet does not exec the plugin. Since Kubernetes 1.24 it asks the CRI runtime to create the sandbox. Common runtimes then load CNI configuration and execute the plugin chain, though CNI does not require that configuration to live on disk. Start with Pod events and kubelet logs. Go to the runtime's logs for plugin detail.

visual.spec: NEW. The real call chain as a sequence: kubelet → CRI → runtime → creates netns → reads CNI config from disk → execs plugin chain. Draw the imagined shortcut from kubelet straight to the plugin and strike it through. Tag each hop with the log you would read if it failed there, and make the runtime's log visually prominent, since that is the one people skip.

beats.title: Where the address comes from
beats.narration: A network plugin can delegate address allocation to an IPAM plugin. That plugin receives the full configuration, and can return addresses, gateways, routes and DNS. Delegation is optional, though. Other implementations allocate through their own node agent instead. So the address does not always come from where you expect.

visual.spec: NEW. A real nested block, not a footnote: the main plugin receives the ADD, and inside it a clearly nested IPAM call that returns address, gateway and routes. The main plugin then applies those to the interface. Render the nesting as genuine containment at full type scale — a previous cut put this detail at 14px grey against an edge and it was the point of the beat. CORRECTION: delegation is optional. Show the delegated path as one option alongside an implementation that allocates through its own node agent.

beats.title: It resolves, nothing answers
beats.narration: DNS resolves and the ClusterIP times out. Check the Service selector, its ports, and its EndpointSlices. Confirm the target process is listening on the resolved endpoint port. From the same source, test the ready Pod address and port directly. If that direct path works, inspect the Service data plane. If it fails, inspect routing, MTU and NetworkPolicy.

visual.spec: NEW. An ordered trace, each step lighting as named, with the check beside it and what a failure there would prove. Step two — testing a Pod address directly — should be visually emphasised as the split point, because it is the step that divides a Service problem from a Pod problem. Lay it out as rows that wrap; do not clip the longer checks.

beats.title: Back to the spine
beats.narration: The CNI segment, then. Ask which path failed. Did the sandbox get an address. Can peers reach that address. Does the Service address reach a ready endpoint. Each answer points at a different owner, and separating them is the whole value. Separate reachability, permission and translation. Each has a different owner and a different log.
